accuracy.evidence: Claims match the research: negative high-arousal emotions narrow attention and the range of actions considered (Fredrickson's broaden-and-build work, shown by the anger dial hiding four calm options), acute stress temporarily impairs prefrontal planning (Arnsten 2009), arousal falls with time so a cooling-off pause helps, and emotions carry decision-relevant signals such as fear flagging danger (Damasio's somatic marker account). The lesson does not claim feelings are bad or that one wait time fits everyone.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the mistakes 9 to 11 year olds make: that feelings should be ignored or bottled up (step 5 prediction, challenge tags ignore and bottle), that a choice made at the peak of anger is the real one (step 3 prediction, tag now), that the situation changed when only the feeling did (tag fact), that being angry makes you bad (tag bad), proving bravery by ignoring fear (tag brave) and choosing before thinking (tag order).

lab_distinct.evidence: flag_cool.js models decision-making under emotion: an anger dial that fades option cards at set thresholds, a hot-versus-cool sort for one scenario, an angry text whose anger meter decays with each 5-minute wait and which punishes sending at the peak, a five-rung stop-think-choose ladder that rejects out-of-order steps, and a listen-or-cool sort. None of it is the triggers, body-clue or stress lab with new labels; it passed the 30% shingle gate.

lab_teaches.evidence: The learner discovers each idea by acting: choices vanish as the dial rises and return as it falls, sending at 10/10 anger produces a hurt reply while waiting 20 minutes lets the calm rewrite through, and the ladder only accepts the plan in order. Done messages confirm what the canvas showed, e.g. 'Hot: only the mean reply and storming off are left.'

predictions.evidence: Three predictions, each with a tempting wrong option: 'When you are furious, do you see more choices or fewer?' (many think anger sharpens thinking), 'After 20 minutes, will the angry text still seem like a good idea?' (yes is tempting at the peak), and 'When you decide, should you ignore your feelings?' (yes is the common taught rule). The lab disproves each and the reveal names the pick.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six rotating questions (Ava's mean comment, why choices shrink, Leo's dare at a busy road, Zoe quitting football, the plan order, the text that looks less rude later). Every wrong option has a tagged message naming the slip, e.g. 'The situation did not change; the feeling did.' and 'Doing something dangerous to look brave is a hot-moment choice.' Choice order rotates.

readability.evidence: Learner audience: kid paragraphs read at FK 2.9 against 6.5 and use concrete scenes (a joke post, a broken Lego tower, an angry text). Adult paragraphs read at FK 6.1 against 9.5 and give scope, evidence, named mistakes and a lab tour. Canvas labels are two to four words with an emoji.

no_filler.evidence: Filler gate passed. Every card carries its own reason (e.g. 'Getting even feels good for a second, then makes things worse.'), every ladder miss explains the right next step, and hints point back to a lab moment (the anger dial, the text you nearly sent) rather than general praise.

mobile.evidence: Checked iPhone 13 (390 px) screenshots in dark and light on every step: the dial and six option cards fit side by side, the phone, clock and anger meter stack in two rows, the plan ladder and loose cards fit in two columns. The dial header was shortened and 'Think what happens next' became 'Think ahead' after both clipped on the first check.

accessibility.evidence: Every drag or tap has a button twin (Hotter, Cooler, bin buttons, Wait 5 minutes, Rewrite calmly, Send, one button per plan step). The canvas aria-label states the anger level, which choices are visible and what is left; feedback is in words, not colour alone; walk.cjs ran axe WCAG 2.1 AA with no violations in light and dark themes on desktop and iPhone 13.
